exercises.title: Setting up Jacobians
exercises.description: Determine the Jacobian of (a) $F_1(x,y) = (x^2 - y,\ x + y^2)$, (b) $F_2(x,y) = (\sin x + y,\ x - \cos y)$, (c) $F_3(x,y) = (e^x - y,\ x^2 + y^2 - 1)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Row $i$ = gradient of $F_i$: $(\partial_xF_i,\ \partial_yF_i)$.

Step 2: (a)
$DF_1 = \begin{pmatrix}2x&-1\\1&2y\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 3: (b)
$DF_2 = \begin{pmatrix}\cos x&1\\1&\sin y\end{pmatrix}$ (since $\partial_y(-\cos y) = \sin y$).

Step 4: (c)
$DF_3 = \begin{pmatrix}e^x&-1\\2x&2y\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Do not transpose: rows are gradients of the component functions, columns belong to the variables.

exercises.title: Evaluating F(x₀)
exercises.description: Evaluate $F(x,y) = (x^2 + y^2 - 4,\ xy - 1)$ and $DF$ at $(1,1)$ and at $(2, 0.5)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Plug into $F$ and $DF = \begin{pmatrix}2x&2y\\y&x\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 2: At (1,1)
$F = (1 + 1 - 4,\ 1 - 1) = (-2, 0)$. $DF = \begin{pmatrix}2&2\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $\det = 0$ – singular!

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Check $\det DF \ne 0$ before the Newton step – at $(1,1)$ it would not be executable.

exercises.title: Setting up the Newton equation
exercises.description: Set up the Newton equation $DF\,\Delta = -F$ for $F(x,y) = (x^2 + y^2 - 4,\ xy - 1)$ at $x_0 = (2, 0.5)$ and solve it.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Use the values from the previous exercise.

Step 2: System
$\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\0.5&2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta_1\\\Delta_2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-0.25\\0\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 3: Solving
Row 2: $\Delta_1 = -4\Delta_2$. Row 1: $-16\Delta_2 + \Delta_2 = -0.25 \Rightarrow \Delta_2 = \frac{1}{60} = 0.016667$, $\Delta_1 = -0.066667$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Right-hand side $-F$ (with the minus), matrix $DF$ (do not invert, solve).

exercises.title: Linear system: one step suffices
exercises.description: Apply Newton to $F(x) = Ax - b$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$, $b = (3,5)^T$ and $x_0 = (0,0)^T$. How many steps are needed?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Here $DF = A$ is constant, $F(x_0) = -b$.

Step 2: Step
$A\Delta = -F(x_0) = b$, so $\Delta = A^{-1}b$ and $x_1 = x_0 + \Delta = A^{-1}b$ – the exact solution.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
For linear $F$ Newton is exact in one step – the linearisation is the function itself.

exercises.title: Locating roots graphically
exercises.description: How many solutions does $x^2 + y^2 = 4$, $xy = 1$ have? Justify graphically and give approximations.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Sketch the circle about the origin with radius $2$ and the hyperbola $y = 1/x$.

Step 2: Sketch
The hyperbola has two branches (1st and 3rd quadrant). Each branch intersects the circle twice (near the $x$- and $y$-axes respectively): $4$ intersections in total.

Step 3: Approximations
From $x^2 + 1/x^2 = 4$: $x^4 - 4x^2 + 1 = 0$, $x^2 = 2\pm\sqrt3$, so $x = \pm1.9319$ or $\pm0.5176$ with $y = 1/x$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
The number of solutions determines how important the starting value is: it selects one of the four.

exercises.title: Stopping criterion
exercises.description: For $x_2 = (1.931853,\ 0.517637)$ we have $F(x_2) = (4.1\cdot10^{-6},\ -1.4\cdot10^{-6})$. Does it satisfy $\|F\|_\infty < 10^{-5}$? What does the last step $\Delta_2$ show?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Check the residual and compare with the step length.

Step 3: Step length
$\Delta_2 = x_2 - x_1 = (-0.00148,\ 0.00097)$, $\|\Delta_2\|_\infty = 1.5\cdot10^{-3}$ – says that the error before the step was $\approx 1.5\cdot10^{-3}$.

Step 4: Conclusion
Because of quadratic convergence the error after the step is much smaller ($\approx 1\cdot10^{-6}$, actually $1.1\cdot10^{-6}$). Use both criteria together.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
For Newton the step length $\|\Delta_k\|$ is a good error estimate for the previous iterate $x_k$.

exercises.title: Symmetric starting value
exercises.description: Why is $x_0 = (1,1)$ an unsuitable starting value for $F = (x^2 + y^2 - 4,\ xy - 1)$? Which starting values are better?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$\det DF = 2x^2 - 2y^2$.

Step 2: Singularity
$\det DF(1,1) = 0$: the system $DF\Delta = -F$ has no unique solution (here none at all: $2\Delta_1 + 2\Delta_2 = 2$ and $\Delta_1 + \Delta_2 = 0$ contradict each other).

Step 3: Better starting values
Points close to an expected solution, e.g. $(2, 0.5)$, $(0.5, 2)$, $(-2,-0.5)$ – away from the lines $y = \pm x$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Symmetry can mean singularity. Shift starting values slightly “out of symmetry”.

exercises.title: Newton versus simplified Newton
exercises.description: Explain the difference between Newton and simplified Newton and state advantages and disadvantages.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The question is whether $DF$ is recomputed in every step.

Step 2: Newton
$DF(x_k)\Delta_k = -F(x_k)$ with new $DF(x_k)$ and a new LU decomposition per step: quadratic convergence, cost $\frac23n^3$ per step.

Step 3: Simplified
$DF(x_0)\Delta_k = -F(x_k)$ with fixed $DF(x_0)$: a single LU decomposition suffices, then only $2n^2$ per step – but only linear convergence.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Worthwhile if $DF$ hardly changes or if function evaluation is cheap and the decomposition expensive.

exercises.title: One full Newton step (2×2)
exercises.description: Perform one Newton step for $F(x,y) = (x^2 + y^2 - 2,\ x - y)$ with $x_0 = (2,1)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$F(x_0)$, $DF(x_0)$, then a linear system.

Step 2: Evaluating
$F(2,1) = (4 + 1 - 2,\ 1) = (3, 1)$. $DF = \begin{pmatrix}2x&2y\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4&2\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 3: System
$\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\Delta = \begin{pmatrix}-3\\-1\end{pmatrix}$. Row 2: $\Delta_1 = \Delta_2 - 1$. Row 1: $4\Delta_2 - 4 + 2\Delta_2 = -3 \Rightarrow \Delta_2 = \frac16$, $\Delta_1 = -\frac56$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The second equation $x - y = 0$ is linear: from $x_1$ on it holds exactly (both components equal).

exercises.title: Second Newton step
exercises.description: Starting from $x_1 = (1.933333,\ 0.516667)$ perform the second Newton step for $F = (x^2 + y^2 - 4,\ xy - 1)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Re-evaluate: $F(x_1)$ and $DF(x_1)$.

Step 4: New point
$x_2 = (1.931852,\ 0.517637)$ – matches the table of the lesson ($1.931853$, $0.517637$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The step length $1.5\cdot10^{-3}$ corresponds to the error of $x_1$ ($1.48\cdot10^{-3}$) – the next error is $\approx 10^{-6}$.

exercises.title: Checking damping
exercises.description: Newton for $F(x) = \arctan x$ with $x_0 = 2$ gives $x_1 = -3.536$. Show that the full step increases $|F|$ and determine the first accepted damping from $\lambda \in \{1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14\}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$\Delta = -F/F' = -\arctan(2)\cdot(1 + 4) = -5.536$; check $|F(x_0 + \lambda\Delta)| < |F(x_0)| = 1.1071$.

Step 4: What next?
From $x = -0.768$ Newton converges with full steps: $x_2 = 0.273$, $x_3 = -0.0134$, $x_4 = 1.6\cdot10^{-6}$ (cubically fast, since $\arctan$ has an inflection point at $0$). Without damping Newton diverges for $|x_0| > 1.39$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Damping = backtracking: halve the step until the objective $\|F\|$ decreases.

exercises.title: Simplified Newton (two steps)
exercises.description: For $F = (x^2 + y^2 - 2,\ x - y)$ with $x_0 = (2,1)$ perform two steps of the simplified Newton method (fixed $DF(x_0)$) and compare with the full method.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
In the first step both agree; afterwards $DF = \begin{pmatrix}4&2\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ stays fixed.

Step 2: Step 1
$x_1 = (1.1667, 1.1667)$ (as for the full method).

Step 4: Comparison
Full: $x_2 = (1.0119, 1.0119)$ (error $0.0119$). Simplified: error $0.0463$. Third step: full $7\cdot10^{-5}$, simplified $0.0147$ – only linear convergence.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The convergence factor of the simplified method is $\approx 0.32$ per step (here $0.0463/0.1667 = 0.28$, $0.0147/0.0463 = 0.32$).

exercises.title: Setting up the Gauss–Newton equation
exercises.description: Set up the Gauss–Newton equation for the model $y = ae^{bt}$ and the data $(0,2), (1,6), (2,17)$ at the starting value $(a,b) = (2,1)$ (without solving it).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Residuals $r_i = y_i - ae^{bt_i}$; $J$ = derivatives of the model with respect to $(a,b)$; $J^TJ\Delta = J^Tr$.

Step 3: Jacobian
$\partial_a = e^{bt}$, $\partial_b = ate^{bt}$: $J = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2.7183&5.4366\\7.3891&29.5562\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 4: Normal equation
$J^TJ = \begin{pmatrix}62.99&233.17\\233.17&903.13\end{pmatrix}$, $J^Tr = \begin{pmatrix}17.95\\68.73\end{pmatrix}$. Solution $\Delta = (0.0730, 0.0573)$, $(a,b)\to(2.073, 1.057)$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The sum of squares drops from $5.254$ to $0.0374$. Watch the conditioning of $J^TJ$: $\mathrm{cond}\approx 10^3$ – use QR if needed.

exercises.title: Recognising a singular Jacobian
exercises.description: At which points is $DF$ of $F = (x^2 + y^2 - 4,\ xy - 1)$ singular? What does this mean geometrically for the intersections of circle and hyperbola?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$\det DF = 2x\cdot x - 2y\cdot y$.

Step 2: Determinant
$\det DF = 2x^2 - 2y^2 = 2(x - y)(x + y) = 0$ on the lines $y = x$ and $y = -x$.

Step 3: Meaning
There the gradients $(2x, 2y)$ and $(y, x)$ are parallel: circle and hyperbola touch (same tangent) – only at $x^2 = y^2$.

Step 4: The solutions
The solutions lie at $y/x = 0.268$ or $3.73$ – not on $y = \pm x$. There $\det DF(x^*) = 2(3.7321 - 0.2679) = 6.93 \ne 0$: nonsingular, Newton converges quadratically.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Singular $DF$ nearby ⇒ huge Newton steps; singular $DF(x^*)$ ⇒ only linear convergence.

exercises.title: Newton for ∇f = 0
exercises.description: Determine the critical points of $f(x,y) = x^2y + y^3 - 3y$ as roots of $\nabla f$. What is the Newton equation and which matrix appears?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$F = \nabla f$, $DF = \nabla^2f$ (Hessian).

Step 2: Gradient
$\nabla f = (2xy,\ x^2 + 3y^2 - 3)$.

Step 3: Hessian
$\nabla^2f = \begin{pmatrix}2y&2x\\2x&6y\end{pmatrix}$ (symmetric).

Step 4: Newton step
$
abla^2f(x_k)\Delta = -
abla f(x_k)$. Example $x_0 = (1, 1)$: $
abla f = (2, 1)$, $
abla^2f =  egin{pmatrix}2&2\2&6\end{pmatrix}$, $\Delta = -	frac{1}{8} egin{pmatrix}6&-2\-2&2\end{pmatrix}(2,1)^T = (-1.25,\ 0.25)$, $x_1 = (-0.25, 1.25)$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
This is Newton's method of optimisation. The Hessian decides the type of critical point (positive definite ⇒ minimum).

exercises.title: Order of convergence from an error sequence
exercises.description: For the circle–hyperbola example the errors are $6.8\cdot10^{-2},\ 1.5\cdot10^{-3},\ 1.1\cdot10^{-6},\ 8\cdot10^{-13}$. Determine the order $p$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$p \approx \dfrac{\ln(e_{k+1}/e_k)}{\ln(e_k/e_{k-1})}$.

Step 4: Conclusion
$p \to 2$: quadratic convergence. The constant: $e_{k+1}/e_k^2 = \frac{1.1\cdot10^{-6}}{(1.5\cdot10^{-3})^2} = 0.49$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
As in 4.7: order from the logarithms of the error ratios; Newton in $\mathbb R^n$ is also quadratic.

exercises.title: Newton for ∇f = 0 as an optimisation method
exercises.description: Show: for $f(x) = \frac12x^TAx - b^Tx$ with symmetric positive definite $A$ Newton's method for $\nabla f = 0$ finds the minimum in one step. What changes for non-quadratic $f$?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Compute gradient and Hessian.

Step 2: Derivatives
$\nabla f(x) = Ax - b$, $\nabla^2f(x) = A$ (constant).

Step 3: Step
$A\Delta = -(Ax_0 - b) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_0 + \Delta = A^{-1}b = x^*$ – exact, wherever you start.

Step 4: Non-quadratic
The Hessian changes: Newton uses the quadratic model $f(x_k) + \nabla f^T\Delta + \tfrac12\Delta^T\nabla^2f\,\Delta$ locally and minimises it. Convergence is quadratic near a minimum, but without damping (line search) and positive definiteness Newton may also run to maxima/saddle points.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Newton minimises the local quadratic model in every step – exact for quadratic objective functions.

exercises.title: Quadratic convergence (sketch)
exercises.description: Sketch the proof of local quadratic convergence of Newton's method in $\mathbb R^n$ under the hypotheses: $F \in C^1$, $DF$ Lipschitz continuous with constant $L$, $DF(x^*)$ nonsingular.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Set up the error recursion $e_{k+1} = x_{k+1} - x^*$ and estimate the remainder of the linear approximation.

Step 2: Recursion
$e_{k+1} = e_k - DF(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k) = DF(x_k)^{-1}\bigl(F(x^*) - F(x_k) - DF(x_k)(x^* - x_k)\bigr)$ (since $F(x^*) = 0$).

Step 3: Remainder
Fundamental theorem of calculus + Lipschitz: $\|F(x^*) - F(x_k) - DF(x_k)(x^* - x_k)\| \le \tfrac L2\|e_k\|^2$.

Step 4: Inverting the derivative
Near $x^*$ we have $\|DF(x_k)^{-1}\| \le 2\|DF(x^*)^{-1}\| =: \beta$ (perturbation theorem for inverses).

Step 5: Result
$\|e_{k+1}\| \le \tfrac{\beta L}{2}\|e_k\|^2$. If $\|e_0\| < \tfrac{2}{\beta L}$ (and within a neighbourhood) then $e_k \to 0$ quadratically. In the example: constant $\approx 0.49$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
The proof is the multidimensional version of 4.7: Taylor remainder + invertibility of the derivative.

exercises.title: Broyden update (one step)
exercises.description: For $F = (x^2 + y^2 - 4,\ xy - 1)$ the first Newton step is $s = (-0.066667, 0.016667)$ from $x_0 = (2, 0.5)$, $F(x_0) = (0.25, 0)$, $F(x_1) = (0.004722, -0.001111)$. Compute $B_1 = B_0 + \frac{(y - B_0s)s^T}{s^Ts}$ with $B_0 = DF(x_0)$ and check the secant condition.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$y = F(x_1) - F(x_0)$; $B_1$ satisfies $B_1s = y$ and differs from $B_0$ only by rank $1$.

Step 4: B₁
$B_1 = \begin{pmatrix}3.93333&1.01667\\0.51569&1.99608\end{pmatrix}$ – hardly different from $DF(x_1) = \begin{pmatrix}3.8667&1.0333\\0.5167&1.9333\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
The update needs only vector operations; with Sherman–Morrison (4.3) one can also obtain the solution of the next system without a new decomposition.

exercises.title: Gauss–Newton for y = a·e^(bt)
exercises.description: Perform a Gauss–Newton step for $y = ae^{bt}$ with the data $(0,2), (1,6), (2,17)$ and start $(2, 1)$ and compute the new sum of squared residuals.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Residuals, $J$, normal equation $J^TJ\Delta = J^Tr$, update, new sum of squares.

Step 2: Residuals and Jacobian
$r = (0,\ 0.5634,\ 2.2219)$, sum of squares $5.2542$. $J = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2.7183&5.4366\\7.3891&29.5562\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 3: Normal equation
$J^TJ = \begin{pmatrix}62.987&233.171\\233.171&903.127\end{pmatrix}$, $J^Tr = \begin{pmatrix}17.949\\68.734\end{pmatrix}$. $\det = 62.987\cdot903.127 - 233.171^2 = 2523.3$.

Step 4: Solution
$\Delta = \tfrac{1}{2523.3}\begin{pmatrix}903.127&-233.171\\-233.171&62.987\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}17.949\\68.734\end{pmatrix} = (0.0730,\ 0.0573)$.

Step 5: New sum of squares
$(a,b) = (2.0730, 1.0573)$: the exact computation gives the new sum of squares $0.0374$ (down from $5.2542$ – a reduction by a factor of $140$).

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Gauss–Newton is almost as good as the optimum here – small residuals at the optimum are the ideal condition.

exercises.title: Basin of convergence: which start, which root?
exercises.description: For $F = (x^2 + y^2 - 4,\ xy - 1)$ Newton leads the starting values $(2,0.5)$, $(0.5,2)$, $(-2,-0.5)$, $(1.5,-1)$, $(3, 0.2)$ to roots. Assign them and explain why $(1.5,-1)$ does not land at a solution in the 4th quadrant.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
There are four solutions, all with $x$ and $y$ of the same sign (because $xy = 1$).

Step 3: (1.5, −1)
In the 4th quadrant ($x > 0, y < 0$) we have $xy < 0 \ne 1$ – there is no solution there. Newton jumps out of that quadrant in the first step and ends at $(1.9319, 0.5176)$.

Step 4: Boundaries
The basins of the four solutions border the lines $y = \pm x$ (where $DF$ is singular): starts near $(1,1.0001)$ land far away ($(-37.8, 40.3)$) and then converge to some solution – the basin is jagged.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The basin of a root is rarely a simple region. Even small changes of the start can lead to other roots.

exercises.title: Newton for z³ = 1 as a 2×2 system
exercises.description: Write $z^3 = 1$ with $z = x + iy$ as the real system $F(x,y) = (x^3 - 3xy^2 - 1,\ 3x^2y - y^3)$ and perform one Newton step from $(1,1)$. Compare with the complex Newton step.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$DF = \begin{pmatrix}3x^2 - 3y^2&-6xy\\6xy&3x^2 - 3y^2\end{pmatrix}$ (Cauchy–Riemann structure).

Step 3: System
$\begin{pmatrix}0&-6\\6&0\end{pmatrix}\Delta = \begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\end{pmatrix}$: $-6\Delta_2 = 3 \Rightarrow \Delta_2 = -\frac12$; $6\Delta_1 = -2 \Rightarrow \Delta_1 = -\frac13$. $x_1 = (0.6667,\ 0.5)$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The basins of the three solutions $1, e^{\pm2\pi i/3}$ form a fractal (Newton fractal) – an extreme case of sensitive dependence on the starting value.

exercises.title: Cost per Newton step
exercises.description: A system with $n = 1000$ unknowns is solved with Newton. Estimate the cost per step if the Jacobian is (a) known analytically, (b) determined by difference quotients ($n+1$ evaluations of $F$ at $10^5$ flops each), and compare with the simplified method.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Costs: $F$ evaluation, Jacobian, LU decomposition ($\frac23n^3$), solve ($2n^2$).

Step 2: (a) analytic
LU: $\frac23\cdot10^9 = 6.7\cdot10^8$. Solve: $2\cdot10^6$. Evaluating $F$ and $DF$: $\approx 10^5 + 10^6$. Total $\approx 6.7\cdot10^8$ flops.

Step 3: (b) Differences
$1001\cdot10^5 = 10^8$ flops extra for $DF$: total $\approx 7.7\cdot10^8$. The decomposition still dominates.

Step 4: Simplified
Once $6.7\cdot10^8$ for the decomposition, then per step only $2\cdot10^6 + 10^5 \approx 2\cdot10^6$ flops. For $10$ steps: $6.9\cdot10^8$ in total instead of $6.7\cdot10^9$ for full Newton – but perhaps $30$ instead of $10$ steps (linear), i.e. $7.3\cdot10^8$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
If the decomposition is expensive, “more but cheaper steps” can win: by a factor of $\approx 10$ here. Broyden lies in between.

exercises.title: Levenberg–Marquardt idea
exercises.description: Explain the Levenberg–Marquardt regularisation $(J^TJ + \mu I)\Delta = J^Tr$ and compute for the exponential model the steps for $\mu = 0, 1, 10$ ($J^TJ$ and $J^Tr$ as above).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
For $\mu = 0$ it is Gauss–Newton, for $\mu \to \infty$ we get $\Delta \approx \frac1\mu J^Tr$ – a gradient step.

Step 3: μ = 1
$\begin{pmatrix}63.99&233.17\\233.17&904.13\end{pmatrix}\Delta = \begin{pmatrix}17.95\\68.73\end{pmatrix}$ ⇒ $\Delta = (0.0579,\ 0.0611)$, $\|\Delta\| = 0.0842$.

Step 4: μ = 10
$\Delta = (0.0296,\ 0.0677)$, $\|\Delta\| = 0.0739$: the step becomes shorter and turns towards the steepest descent $J^Tr \propto (17.95, 68.73)$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
LM is a trust-region method: $\mu$ is increased if a step does not reduce the sum of squares and decreased if it was good. Robust for bad starting values.
